```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, fig.align = "center",
                      comment = "#>")
navy   <- "#13294B"
accent <- "#4B9CD3"
hl     <- "#D35400"
```

These simulations go with the slides at [thevazquezlab.com/talks](https://thevazquezlab.com/talks). Every chunk runs in base R; copy and paste the code to try other values.

# 1. The binomial distribution

Our clinic example: $n = 4$ patients, and each one tests positive with probability $p = 0.25$.

```{r binom-basics}
n <- 4
p <- 0.25

dbinom(0:n, size = n, prob = p)   # P(X = k) for k = 0, ..., 4
choose(4, 1)                      # number of ways to get exactly one positive
pbinom(1, size = n, prob = p)     # P(X <= 1)
c(mean = n * p, variance = n * p * (1 - p))
```

```{r binom-pmf, fig.height = 3.6}
barplot(dbinom(0:n, n, p), names.arg = 0:n, col = accent, border = NA,
        xlab = "Number of positive tests, k", ylab = "P(X = k)",
        main = "Binomial(n = 4, p = 0.25)")
```

# 2. The jar

My jar holds $N = 126$ objects. After the first toss I swapped in $M = 21$ blue cubes. On the second toss $n = 21$ objects land inside the circle, and each one is a cube with probability $p = M/N$. The number of cubes in the circle, $X$, is binomial, and the Lincoln–Petersen estimator is $\hat N = Mn/k$.

```{r jar-one}
set.seed(2026)
N <- 126   # true total (unknown in practice)
M <- 21    # cubes swapped in
n <- 21    # objects in the circle on the second toss

k <- rbinom(1, size = n, prob = M / N)   # cubes in the circle
k
M * n / k                                # one estimate of N
```

Now repeat the experiment 1,000 times.

```{r jar-sim}
R <- 1000
k <- rbinom(R, size = n, prob = M / N)
N_hat <- ifelse(k > 0, M * n / k, NA)

summary(N_hat)
quantile(N_hat, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)   # middle 90% of the estimates
mean(k == 0)                                   # share of jars with no cubes in the circle
```

```{r jar-hist}
hist(N_hat, breaks = seq(0, 1500, by = 10), xlim = c(40, 470),
     col = accent, border = "white", main = "1,000 simulated jars",
     xlab = expression(hat(N) == Mn/k), ylab = "Number of jars")
abline(v = N, col = hl, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
text(N + 10, par("usr")[4] * 0.9, "true N = 126", col = hl, adj = 0)
```

The estimates pile up near 126 but have a long right tail: tosses with few cubes in the circle give very large estimates. Because $k$ is a whole number, $\hat N = 441/k$ takes only a few values, and a toss with $k = 0$ gives no estimate at all.

# 3. My jar at home: 28 real tosses

I ran the experiment 28 times with the real jar ($N = 126$, $M = 21$). For each toss I counted the pebbles and the cubes inside the circle.

```{r home-data}
pebbles <- c(20, 6, 18, 16, 15, 12, 15, 18, 11, 21, 11, 16, 13, 17,
             13, 23, 16, 12, 15, 14, 15, 16, 16, 24, 17, 18, 8, 17)
cubes   <- c(2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 1, 0, 2, 3,
             3, 2, 3, 4, 3, 1, 1, 3, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 3)
n_home <- pebbles + cubes                  # all objects in the circle
N_home <- ifelse(cubes > 0, 21 * n_home / cubes, NA)

median(N_home, na.rm = TRUE)               # median estimate
21 * sum(n_home) / sum(cubes)              # pooled estimate
sum(cubes) / sum(n_home)                   # share of cubes in the circle (jar: 21/126 = 0.167)
```

The real estimates run a little high: cubes were 14% of the objects in the circle but 17% of the jar, so cubes were somewhat less likely than pebbles to land in the circle.

# 4. What does a bigger second toss buy?

```{r jar-n, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 3.8}
sim_jar <- function(n, R = 1000) {
  k <- rbinom(R, size = n, prob = M / N)
  ifelse(k > 0, M * n / k, NA)
}
est_21 <- N_hat          # the 1,000 jars from section 2
est_60 <- sim_jar(60)

rbind("n = 21" = quantile(est_21, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
      "n = 60" = quantile(est_60, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE))
c("n = 21" = sum(is.na(est_21)), "n = 60" = sum(is.na(est_60)))   # jars with no cubes in the circle

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (v in list(list(est_21, "Second toss n = 21"), list(est_60, "Second toss n = 60"))) {
  hist(v[[1]], breaks = seq(0, 1500, by = 10), xlim = c(40, 470), col = accent,
       border = "white", main = v[[2]], xlab = expression(hat(N)), ylab = "Number of jars")
  abline(v = N, col = hl, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
}
```

A bigger second toss narrows the spread of the estimates around the true total.

# 5. Two clinics

Now the "jar" is a population of $N = 180$ people. Clinic A's list plays the role of the cubes ($M$), clinic B's list plays the role of the second toss ($n$), and people on both lists are the cubes in the circle ($k$). The function below simulates both lists under four scenarios.

```{r clinics-fun}
sim_clinics <- function(scenario, N = 180, R = 1000) {
  est <- numeric(R)
  for (r in 1:R) {
    if (scenario == "Independent lists") {
      a <- runif(N) < 1/3
      b <- runif(N) < 1/4
    } else if (scenario == "Referral") {
      # people on A's list are often referred to B
      a <- runif(N) < 1/3
      b <- ifelse(a, runif(N) < 0.5, runif(N) < 0.167)
    } else if (scenario == "Hard-to-reach group") {
      # 60 people rarely reach either clinic
      hard <- seq_len(N) <= 60
      a <- runif(N) < ifelse(hard, 0.10, 0.43)
      b <- runif(N) < ifelse(hard, 0.10, 0.33)
    } else if (scenario == "Separate catchments") {
      # half live near clinic B, half near clinic A
      near_b <- seq_len(N) <= N / 2
      a <- runif(N) < ifelse(near_b, 0.10, 0.55)
      b <- runif(N) < ifelse(near_b, 0.50, 0.10)
    }
    k <- sum(a & b)
    est[r] <- if (k > 0) sum(a) * sum(b) / k else NA
  }
  est
}
```

```{r clinics-run}
set.seed(2026)
scenarios <- c("Independent lists", "Referral", "Hard-to-reach group", "Separate catchments")
res <- lapply(scenarios, sim_clinics)
names(res) <- scenarios

data.frame(median = sapply(res, median, na.rm = TRUE),
           share_below_180 = sapply(res, function(v) mean(v < 180, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

```{r clinics-hist, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 3.6}
par(mfrow = c(1, 4))
for (s in scenarios) {
  hist(pmin(res[[s]], 610), breaks = seq(40, 620, by = 20), col = accent,
       border = "white", main = s, xlab = expression(hat(N)), ylab = "Number of simulations")
  abline(v = 180, col = hl, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
}
```

When the two lists are independent, the estimates center on the true total of 180. Referral and a hard-to-reach group make the lists overlap too much, so the estimator falls short; separate catchments make the lists overlap too little, so the estimator overshoots.
